Pension income splitting: test the 50% election against 2026 brackets, credits and the OAS clawback

A worked guide to the CRA pension income splitting election: which income is eligible, why CPP and OAS stay put, how the age amount, pension income amount and OAS recovery tax react, and why the best allocation is not always 50%. Five charts and an editable 2026 federal model.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Test a pension income splitting election with 2026 federal rules

Original federal-only illustration for the 2026 tax year using CRA’s 2026 federal brackets (14%, 20.5%, 26%, 29%, 33%), the 2026 basic personal amount (CAD 16,452 phasing to CAD 14,829 between CAD 181,440 and CAD 258,482), the 2026 age amount (CAD 9,208 reduced by 15% of net income above CAD 46,432), the CAD 2,000 federal pension income amount and the 2026-income OAS recovery threshold of CAD 95,323. Both spouses are assumed to be 65 or older on 31 December 2026, resident in Canada and not separated. Net income equals the entered income; there are no other deductions or credits, no provincial tax, and no dividend, capital-gain or foreign-income rules. OAS recovery for 2026 income is collected through the return and later OAS payments; it is counted here in one total. The result is not tax advice or a filing calculation.

The central idea

Splitting moves up to half of eligible pension income from one return to the other; household income does not change. The saving comes from rate differences, credits and clawbacks between the two spouses, so the right percentage depends on both incomes and can be zero.

01

The election moves income between two returns, not out of the household

Pension income splitting lets a spouse or common-law partner who receives eligible pension income allocate up to 50% of it to the other spouse for tax purposes. No money changes accounts. The transferring spouse deducts the elected split-pension amount on line 21000, and the receiving spouse reports the same amount on line 11600. Both spouses complete Form T1032 with matching figures and file it with their returns by the filing due date.

The CRA lists four conditions: the couple were married or living common-law in the year; they were not living separate and apart because of a breakdown of the relationship for a continuous 90 days or more that includes 31 December; both were resident in Canada on 31 December (or at death); and the transferring spouse received income that qualifies for the pension income amount. Only one joint election can be made each year, and the percentage can change from one year to the next.

Because household net income is unchanged, the election helps only when the same dollars attract less tax, more credits or a smaller benefit clawback on the receiving spouse’s return. If both spouses already sit in the same position, moving income does nothing—or can cost money.

02

Which pension dollars qualify—and the age-65 dividing line

The CRA describes eligible pension income as the taxable part of life-annuity payments from a registered pension plan or other superannuation fund at any age. RRIF and LIF payments, RRSP annuity payments, other annuity payments and certain retirement compensation arrangement amounts count only if the transferring spouse is 65 or older at the end of the year, or if the payments arise from the death of a spouse. Variable benefits from a money-purchase provision or a pooled registered pension plan follow the same 65-or-death condition.

Several common retirement incomes cannot be split at all: Old Age Security, CPP and QPP, US IRA payments, foreign pensions that are tax-free in Canada under a treaty, and RRIF amounts transferred to an RRSP, another RRIF or an annuity. CPP has a separate “pension sharing” process administered by Service Canada; it is not part of the T1032 election and is not modelled here.

Eligibility summary from CRA guidance (reviewed 26 October 2026)
IncomeTransferring spouse under 65Transferring spouse 65+
RPP life annuityEligibleEligible
RRIF / LIF paymentsOnly if from a spouse’s deathEligible
RRSP annuityOnly if from a spouse’s deathEligible
Lump-sum RRSP withdrawalNot eligibleNot eligible
CPP / QPP, OASNot eligibleNot eligible

The receiving spouse’s age does not affect whether the election can be made. It can affect what that spouse may claim: CRA’s line 31400 chart treats the split amount as qualifying for the receiving spouse’s pension income amount, with Form T1032 step 4 governing the calculation when the receiving spouse is under 65.

03

Worked example: CAD 95,000 and CAD 16,000 become CAD 60,000 and CAD 51,000

Take a hypothetical couple, both 65 or older on 31 December 2026. Alex receives a CAD 70,000 registered pension and CAD 25,000 of CPP and OAS (CAD 9,150 of it OAS—12 months at the October–December 2026 maximum of CAD 762.50, held flat). Sam has CAD 16,000 of CPP and OAS and no pension. Net incomes: CAD 95,000 and CAD 16,000.

Without splitting, Alex’s 2026 federal bracket tax is CAD 15,671.01 (CAD 58,523 at 14% plus CAD 36,477 at 20.5%). The 2026 credits are the CAD 16,452 basic personal amount, an age amount reduced to CAD 1,922.80 (CAD 9,208 minus 15% of the CAD 48,568 above CAD 46,432) and the CAD 2,000 pension income amount, all at 14%: CAD 2,852.47. Alex owes CAD 12,818.53. Sam’s credits exceed Sam’s CAD 2,240 of bracket tax, so Sam owes nothing—and CAD 1,352.40 of Sam’s credits go unused because they are non-refundable.

Allocating 50% (CAD 35,000) gives Alex CAD 60,000 and Sam CAD 51,000. Alex now owes CAD 4,908.53 and Sam CAD 3,363.53: CAD 8,272.06 together, an illustrative federal saving of CAD 4,546.47. The bridge chart breaks that into CAD 2,275.00 of lower bracket tax, CAD 639.07 of additional age-amount value, CAD 280.00 from Sam’s new pension income amount and CAD 1,352.40 of credits Sam can now actually use. Provincial tax would change the dollar figures and is excluded.

04

Why the best percentage is sometimes below 50%—or zero

Splitting saves money only while the receiving spouse’s combined marginal cost is lower than the transferring spouse’s. Once the two incomes sit in the same bracket and outside credit phase-outs, each extra dollar moved saves nothing, so the cost curve goes flat. Move further and the receiving spouse can cross into a higher bracket, past the CAD 46,432 point where the age amount starts shrinking, or above the CAD 95,323 OAS recovery threshold for 2026 income.

Three original scenarios from the model illustrate the range. With Alex’s pension raised to CAD 100,000 (net income CAD 125,000), Alex would face OAS recovery tax of CAD 4,451.55 (15% of CAD 29,677) without splitting; allocating about 30% brings Alex below the threshold and removes it, and the modelled federal saving keeps rising to CAD 9,563.73 at 43% before the curve goes flat. If Alex has CAD 60,000 of pension plus CAD 25,000 and Sam already has CAD 50,000 including a CAD 20,000 pension, the saving reaches about CAD 554 at 15%, stays flat through 44%, then falls to CAD 325.00 at 50%: beyond 44% Alex drops into the 14% band while Sam is still taxed at 20.5% on each extra dollar. If both start at CAD 60,000, splitting 50% of a CAD 40,000 pension costs CAD 1,339.07 more than not splitting, because it pushes Sam into the 20.5% band and shrinks Sam’s age amount.

The model reports the smallest whole percentage that reaches the lowest modelled cost. Where the curve is flat, other considerations—instalments, withholding, provincial credits, income-tested benefits—decide where in the flat range a household lands.

05

Withholding follows the pension, not the election

The election does not change who receives the payment or the tax withheld at source. The CRA requires tax withheld on eligible pension income to be allocated between spouses in the same proportion as the pension, and it cannot approve reduced withholding because a split is planned. When a slip mixes eligible and non-eligible pension income, the withheld tax on the eligible part is the eligible share of the total multiplied by total tax withheld.

Example: if CAD 14,000 was withheld on Alex’s CAD 70,000 pension and 50% is allocated, CAD 7,000 of that withholding moves to Sam’s return through line 43700. Sam may still owe a balance or receive a refund depending on Sam’s own tax; the household can also face CRA instalment reminders if net tax owing exceeds the instalment threshold in successive years. The household cash-flow plan should allow for that timing rather than assume withholding already matches each return.

06

Deadlines, late elections and a checklist before filing

The T1032 election belongs with the returns for the year and must be filed by the filing due date. The CRA says it may accept a late or amended election, or a revocation, if requested within three calendar years after the filing due date, and both spouses must agree. An amendment needs a new jointly signed T1032; a revocation needs a letter signed by both.

Before choosing a percentage: confirm the income is eligible for the transferring spouse’s age; check both spouses’ net income against the age-amount, OAS recovery and bracket markers in the chart below; consider income-tested benefits such as GIS that use net income; include provincial or territorial tax and credits; and check whether medical-expense or other credits that depend on net income change. Tax software usually optimizes the split automatically, but the result is only as good as the slips and inputs entered.

The interactive model is a federal-only teaching tool for the 2026 tax year. It assumes both spouses are 65 or older, resident, not separated and without other deductions or credits. It does not include provincial tax, dividend gross-up, capital gains, the CPP enhanced-contribution deduction, GIS or other benefits. Use it to understand the mechanics and to frame questions for a tax professional—not to file.
